claims.text: Increasing Cr and/or Al content in a multiprincipal-element alloy promotes formation of a continuous, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide scale.
Formation of the protective oxide scale improves oxidation resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
Formation of the protective oxide scale preserves material integrity at high temperature relative to the baseline alloy.
The baseline is a standard multiprincipal-element alloy with typical refractory-metal content and without enhanced reactive-element segregation.
Cr and Al form stable, protective oxides.
A continuous and adherent Cr2O3 or Al2O3 layer acts as a barrier against further oxidation.
Higher reactive-element content enables reactive elements to segregate to the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
Surface segregation of reactive elements causes early formation of a uniform, slow-growing oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale minimizes oxygen ingress.
The protective oxide scale reduces internal oxidation and scale spallation.
Reduced oxygen ingress, internal oxidation, and scale spallation maintain matrix integrity under thermal and mechanical stresses.
The reactive-element-enhanced alloy will have a lower oxide-scale growth rate than the baseline.
The reactive-element-enhanced alloy will exhibit less scale spallation than the baseline.
The reactive-element-enhanced alloy will retain its microstructural and mechanical integrity better than the baseline after oxidation.
The proposed comparison applies approximately over 900–1100 °C in oxidizing environments.
Applicability outside 900–1100 °C or in different oxidizing atmospheres is uncertain.
The exact improvement in oxide thickness and mechanical-property retention may vary with reactive-element effectiveness and alloy processing.
